# 🎂 Amazing Birthday — February 29, 1960

You were born on a Monday. Dwight D. Eisenhower was president, though his last year was almost up — a young senator from Massachusetts was already eyeing the White House. The Cold War was humming at full tension. Rock and roll was two years past its first revolution and about to start its second.

And you were born on a date that doesn't exist most of the time.

---

## 📅 You have had 16 birthdays

At 66 years old, you have celebrated February 29th exactly sixteen times.

You are what's called a *leapling* — one of roughly 5 million people alive today born on the rarest date on the calendar, a day that appears only when the Earth's orbit demands correction. February 29 exists because a solar year is 365.2422 days, and without the leap day, our calendar would drift a full month out of alignment with the seasons in just 130 years. You are, in a literal sense, a calendrical correction.

Most years, your birthday doesn't exist. For three years out of four, the world simply skips past the date you arrived. Different countries have different laws about this: some say February 28th is your legal birthday in non-leap years, some say March 1st. Neither is correct. The date is simply *absent*.

Your next real birthday — February 29 on an actual calendar — is February 29, 2028. You'll be 68 years old and celebrating your 17th birthday.

---

## 🏔️ A city was destroyed the night you were born

At 11:47 PM on February 29, 1960, a powerful earthquake struck Agadir, Morocco. It lasted just fifteen seconds. The city — one of Morocco's most beautiful, a resort on the Atlantic coast — was almost entirely destroyed. Approximately 12,000 people were killed, roughly a third of Agadir's entire population.

The earthquake's devastation was compounded by its shallow depth: the shaking was extraordinarily intense at the surface, and most of the city's buildings collapsed instantly. King Mohammed V declared three days of national mourning. Agadir was rebuilt from scratch over the following decade — a completely new city, planned from the ground up, rising from rubble on the same shoreline.

You arrived into the world on the same night a city ceased to exist and began its long effort to become itself again.

---

## ☕ The Civil Rights Movement took its decisive turn 28 days before you were born

On February 1, 1960 — four weeks before your birthday — four Black college students sat down at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave when denied service. They were polite. They were dressed impeccably. They sat until closing time, returned the next morning with more students, and sparked a movement.

Within weeks, sit-ins had spread to dozens of cities across the South. Within months, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee was founded. The Greensboro sit-ins didn't end segregation — but they changed the strategy, the urgency, and the visibility of the Civil Rights Movement in ways that made everything that followed possible.

You were born into a country that was already, visibly, changing. By the time you were old enough to understand what country you lived in, the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) had been signed. The world your parents were born into was not the world you grew up in — and that shift was already underway the month you arrived.

---

## 💊 The birth control pill was approved three months after your birthday

On May 9, 1960, the FDA approved Enovid — the first oral contraceptive — for use in the United States. You were ten weeks old.

It's difficult to overstate what followed. The Pill restructured the relationship between women and their own lives: when and whether to have children, whether to pursue careers, how to think about marriage and independence. It reshaped medicine, family formation, gender politics, and culture across the following six decades.

You were born just before one of the most consequential medical approvals in American history. The world your generation of women grew up in — with choices their mothers never had — took its first legal step when you were barely out of the hospital.

---

## 🎸 Elvis came home from the Army the month after your birthday, and The Beatles were forming in Liverpool

On March 5, 1960 — four days after your first week of life — Elvis Presley returned from two years of military service in Germany. He'd been drafted in 1958, and the music world had held its breath. He was 25. He filmed his comeback television appearance almost immediately and released "Stuck on You" within weeks. Rock and roll exhaled.

Meanwhile, in Liverpool, a group called the Quarrymen was transforming into something else. In 1960, they played Hamburg for the first time, cycled through band names, and finally settled on *The Beatles*. John Lennon was 19. Paul McCartney was 17. George Harrison was 16.

You were born at the exact hinge between the first generation of rock and roll and its second, larger wave. By the time you were four, the Beatles had arrived in America.

---

## 🌍 1960 was the Year Africa Was Born

Seventeen African nations declared independence in 1960 — more than in any other year in history. Nigeria. Senegal. Mali. Côte d'Ivoire. Cameroon. The Democratic Republic of Congo. The map of an entire continent rewrote itself the year you arrived.

At the United Nations, the African bloc went from a handful of nations to a major force almost overnight. The decolonization of the world — the largest political transformation of the twentieth century — was at its peak. You were born into its most concentrated moment.

---

# 🌎 The world you were born into

When you arrived, the world had:

- **No Berlin Wall.** It went up in August 1961, when you were one year old — the first wall of your conscious life. It fell in November 1989, when you were 29.
- **No human being who had been to space.** Yuri Gagarin went up in April 1961. You were just over a year old.
- **No Beatles records.** *Please Please Me* came out in 1963. You were three.
- **Seventeen new African nations** and counting.
- **No internet, no mobile phones, no GPS.**
- **Eisenhower as president.** You would live through twelve more.

In your lifetime, you have watched:

- The Moon landing, age 9 (your third leap-year birthday was still five years away)
- The Berlin Wall rise *and* fall — the entire arc, bookended in your lifetime
- The assassinations of JFK, MLK, and RFK, all before age 9
- Watergate, age 13
- The AIDS epidemic reshape an entire generation
- The internet transform every aspect of human life
- 9/11, age 41
- The first Black U.S. president, age 48
- A global pandemic, age 60

And through all of it, you have technically celebrated your birthday sixteen times.

You were born on a day that barely exists — which is exactly right for someone born into a year that remade the world.
